query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Cryogenic rolling of eutectic high-entropy alloys followed by a controlled low‐temperature annealing step can simultaneously enhance yield strength and room-temperature ductility by refining the dual-phase lamellar colonies and activating in‐situ microcrack arresting mechanisms.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation
generation.intervention: Apply cryogenic rolling (i.e., severe deformation at cryogenic temperatures) followed by optimized low-temperature annealing
generation.conditions: Processing should involve a high degree of deformation (e.g., ~90% thickness reduction by cryo-rolling) and subsequent annealing at a temperature low enough to avoid significant grain coarsening yet high enough to relax residual stresses; tensile tests at room temperature
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrafine, hierarchically heterogeneous duplex microstructure with refined lamellae, reduced grain sizes, and enhanced phase boundary coherency that promotes microcrack arrest
generation.mechanism: Cryogenic deformation increases dislocation density and fragments the original coarse lamellar structure into ultrafine regions, which, when partially recrystallized during controlled annealing, preserves fine lamellae. This refined microstructure enhances strength via grain boundary and precipitation strengthening while the high density of obstacles at phase boundaries impedes crack propagation, leading to improved ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified as-cast lamellar baseline, the treated alloy is expected to exhibit higher yield and ultimate tensile strength alongside an increased uniform elongation, with microstructural observations revealing refined lamellae and evidence of microcrack arrest
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with coarse dual-phase lamellar colonies that are susceptible to microcrack initiation and brittle room-temperature tensile behavior
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective when the cryogenic deformation is sufficiently severe and the subsequent annealing parameters (temperature and duration) are optimized to avoid excessive grain growth; the alloy composition must be conducive to maintaining lamellar stability after processing
generation.uncertainty: Exact improvements in mechanical properties and the optimal processing parameters depend on alloy composition and may vary; the degree to which microcrack arrest mechanisms contribute requires further quantification

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same eutectic high-entropy alloy composition. Process one set using conventional rolling and annealing, and process the second set by applying cryogenic rolling (targeting high reduction, e.g., ~90%) followed by a controlled low-temperature annealing treatment. Perform detailed microstructural characterization (using TEM/SEM) and conduct room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests on both sets.
measurements: Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure
Grain and lamellar size distributions via microscopy
Dislocation density and evidence for microcrack arrest (e.g., crack bridging or deflection)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cryo-rolled and annealed samples do not simultaneously exhibit both statistically significant increases in strength and ductility relative to the conventionally processed control and lack the refined hierarchical microstructure with features that arrest microcrack propagation, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Simultaneous Strength-Ductility Enhancement of a Nano-Lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High Entropy Alloy by Cryo-Rolling and Annealing

Abstract: Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. Enhanced strength–ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae

Abstract: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism.
